rewritten_text:
“I’m dining out, so I won’t need you.”

“Thank you, sir,” the man said, leaving.

“Now, Alan, we can’t waste a moment. What a heavy chest! I’ll carry it. You take the other things.” His words were quick and commanding. Campbell felt himself under Dorian’s control. They went out together.

At the top landing, Dorian took out the key and unlocked the door. Then he stopped, his eyes suddenly troubled. He shuddered. “I don’t think I can go inside, Alan,” he murmured.

“That makes no difference to me. I don’t need you,” Campbell replied coldly.

Dorian opened the door halfway. As he did, he saw the face in his portrait leering in the sunlight. The torn curtain lay on the floor before it. He remembered that the previous night, for the first time in his life, he had forgotten to cover the fatal canvas. He was about to rush forward when he recoiled with a shudder.

What was that disgusting red moisture shining on one of the hands, wet and glistening as though the painting had sweated blood? How horrifying it was! For a moment it seemed even more terrible than the silent thing he knew lay across the table. Its grotesque, distorted shadow on the stained carpet told him it had not moved. It remained exactly where he had left it.

He drew a deep breath, pushed the door farther open, and hurried inside with his eyes half closed and his head turned away. He was determined not to look at the dead man even once. Bending down, he picked up the gold-and-purple curtain and threw it over the portrait.

He stopped there, afraid to turn around, staring at the intricate pattern in front of him. He heard Campbell carrying in the heavy chest, the iron implements, and the other materials he had requested for his dreadful work. Dorian began wondering whether Campbell and Basil Hallward had ever met and, if so, what each had thought of the other.

“Leave me now,” said a stern voice behind him.

He turned and rushed out, barely registering that the body had been pushed back into the chair and Campbell was staring into a shiny yellow face. As he went downstairs, he heard the key turn in the lock.

It was well past seven when Campbell returned to the library. He was pale but completely composed. “I’ve done what you asked,” he muttered.

“But the thought that sustained me at the outset of my course now merely presses me deeper into the dust. My theories and expectations have come to nothing, and, like the archangel who coveted omnipotence, I am bound within an everlasting hell. My fancy was lively, but my powers of reasoning and sustained labour were equally strong; together they enabled me to conceive and accomplish the creation of a man. Even now I cannot remember without emotion the dreams that accompanied my unfinished work. In imagination I walked through heaven, rejoicing now in my abilities, now burning at the prospect of their consequences. From childhood great hopes and exalted ambition possessed me; yet how low I have fallen! My friend, had you known me in those days, you would scarcely recognize this degraded being. Despair seldom entered my heart. A mighty destiny seemed to carry me onward until I fell, never, never to rise again.”

Must I lose this admirable creature, then? I have yearned for a friend, sought someone who would understand and love me. Here, upon these deserted seas, I have found him; yet I fear I have gained him only long enough to learn his worth before losing him. I would restore his attachment to life, but he rejects the thought.

“I thank you, Walton,” he said, “for your kindness towards one so wretched. But when you speak of fresh attachments and new affections, do you believe anyone can replace the dead? Can any man become another Clerval to me, or any woman another Elizabeth? Even without exceptional virtues to engage our love, the friends of childhood hold a certain influence over our minds that later companions can scarcely achieve. They understand our earliest dispositions, which may change but are never wholly removed, and can therefore judge our conduct with greater confidence in the honesty of our intentions. Unless signs appeared in youth, a brother or sister can hardly suspect the other of deceit or treachery, while a later friend, however affectionate, may despite himself be regarded with mistrust. But my friends were precious not only through familiarity and shared experience, but through their own excellence. Wherever I go, Elizabeth’s comforting voice and Clerval’s conversation will whisper in my ears. They are dead, and in this loneliness only one feeling can induce me to keep living. Were I occupied with some noble enterprise or purpose promising great benefit to my fellow beings, I could live to complete it.

I told myself I wanted nothing to do with business like that.

When I came downstairs the next morning, the parlor was closed and the people who had sat up with the body were gone. Only the family, the widow Bartley, and our bunch were there. I studied their faces to see whether anything had happened, but learned nothing.

Around midday the undertaker arrived with his assistant. They placed the coffin on two chairs in the middle of the room, then arranged all our chairs in rows. They borrowed more from the neighbors until the hall, parlor, and dining room were full. The coffin lid was positioned just as before, but with everyone around I didn’t dare peek underneath.

People began pouring in. The swindlers and the girls sat in the front row at the head of the coffin. For half an hour, the visitors passed slowly in single file, each pausing to look down at the dead man’s face. Some let a tear fall. Everything was very quiet and solemn, apart from the girls and the swindlers holding handkerchiefs to their eyes, bowing their heads, and sobbing a little. The only other noises were shoes scraping the floor and people blowing their noses. People always blow their noses more at funerals than anywhere else, except church.

Once the place was packed, the undertaker glided around in black gloves, quietly and soothingly adding the final touches. He arranged the people and furniture until everything was orderly and everyone comfortable, making no more noise than a cat. He never said a word. With nods and hand signals, he moved people, squeezed in late arrivals, and cleared paths through the crowd. Then he stood against the wall. He was the quietest, smoothest, sneakiest-moving man I had ever seen, and he had about as much smile in him as a ham.

They had borrowed a small pump organ, and it sounded sick. When everything was ready, a young woman sat down to play. The thing squealed and groaned, and everyone joined in singing. In my opinion, Peter was the only one who had the best of it. Then the Reverend Hobson began speaking in a slow, solemn voice. Immediately, the most outrageous noise anyone ever heard erupted in the cellar. Only one dog was making it, but what a tremendous racket! He kept it up without stopping. The minister had to stand over the coffin and wait. You couldn’t hear yourself think.
